title: Joel 2:1–11
context: The prophet calls for an alarm on Zion, for “the day of the LORD comes” (2:1). He describes a day of darkness and a vast people that advances like an army: fire before them, a ruined land behind them, the earth quaking and the heavens darkened (2:2–10). In 2:11 the LORD himself leads this army. Readers in both traditions take the army as the locusts of chapter 1 described in military images, as a human invader foreshadowed by them, or as a picture of the final day of the LORD; many combine these readings. Joel’s description of the day echoes other prophets, compare Zephaniah 1:14–15 and Amos 5:18–20. Shared ground: both traditions read the unit as an urgent warning that the LORD’s day is fearful, ending with the question “who can endure it?”

verses.text: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD comes, for it is close at hand:
verses.arminianNotes: Joel calls for the trumpet in Zion and an alarm on the holy mountain, for the day of the LORD is near. Arminian readers see the alarm as a merciful warning, giving people time to prepare and turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trumpet as the watchman’s signal of approaching judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as urgent proclamation, with the day of the LORD understood in historical, typological, and future senses.

verses.text: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.
verses.arminianNotes: The day is darkness and gloom, and a great people comes like dawn on the mountains, unlike any before or after. Arminian readers note the echo of Exodus 10:14, where the locusts of Egypt were also without equal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the darkness imagery as typical of the day of the LORD, compare Zephaniah 1:15 by reference. Both traditions read the great people as the locust army or an invading host it foreshadows, holding these readings together.

verses.text: A fire devours before them, and behind them, a flame burns. The land is as the garden of Eden before them, and behind them, a desolate wilderness. Yes, and no one has escaped them.
verses.arminianNotes: Fire devours before them and flame behind; the land is like Eden before them and a desolate wilderness after. Arminian readers see the reversal of paradise into wasteland, a vivid picture of destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast with the promise of a land made like Eden, compare Ezekiel 36:35 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the image as showing how the advancing army undoes the land’s beauty and abundance.

verses.text: Their appearance is as the appearance of horses, and they run as horsemen.
verses.arminianNotes: Their appearance is like horses, and they run like horsemen. Arminian readers note that locusts’ heads have often been compared to horses, making the image fitting for an insect army.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the military comparison emphasizing speed and power. Both traditions read the verse as part of a poetic description that joins insect and army images, without forcing it to a single referent.

verses.text: Like the noise of chariots on the tops of the mountains, they leap, like the noise of a flame of fire that devours the stubble, like a strong people set in battle array.
verses.arminianNotes: They leap like chariots on the mountains and sound like fire devouring stubble, like an army in battle array. Arminian readers see the noise of the swarm described in terms that inspire terror.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse building the picture of an unstoppable force under God’s command. Shared ground: both traditions read the layered similes as heightening the sense of approaching danger.

verses.text: At their presence the peoples are in anguish. All faces have grown pale.
verses.arminianNotes: At their presence the peoples are in anguish, and every face grows pale. Arminian readers see the human response of fear, as people recognize their helplessness before the advance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the anguish as the fitting response to the approach of the LORD’s judgment. Both traditions read the verse as conveying the dread that the day of the LORD brings to all who face it.

verses.text: They run like mighty men. They climb the wall like warriors. They each march in his line, and they don’t swerve off course.
verses.arminianNotes: They run like mighty men, climb walls like warriors, and march in line without swerving. Arminian readers note the disciplined movement, which makes the army seem purposeful and directed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the order of the army as reflecting the one who commands it, as 2:11 will make clear. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as portraying a force that no wall can stop.

verses.text: One doesn’t jostle another. They each march in their own path. They burst through the defenses and don’t break ranks.
verses.arminianNotes: They do not jostle one another, burst through defenses, and keep their ranks. Arminian readers see a picture of relentless advance, each moving in its own path toward its goal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precision as a sign of divine direction behind the scene. Both traditions read the verse as continuing the military portrait, and they hold its locust and human readings side by side.

verses.text: They rush on the city. They run on the wall. They climb up into the houses. They enter in at the windows like thieves.
verses.arminianNotes: They rush the city, run on the wall, climb into houses, and enter windows like thieves. Arminian readers see the invasion reaching even private homes, leaving no place of refuge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as showing that judgment penetrates every barrier. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as realistic of locust swarms and evocative of invading armies alike.

verses.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
verses.arminianNotes: The earth quakes, the heavens tremble, and sun, moon, and stars are darkened. Arminian readers see cosmic language describing the magnitude of the day, compare Isaiah 13:10 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shaking of creation as a common feature of the day of the LORD in the prophets. Both traditions read the verse as poetic description that may also point to final judgment, and they keep these readings together.

verses.text: The LORD thunders his voice before his army, for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of the LORD is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD thunders before his army, for his forces are great, and the day of the LORD is awesome; who can endure it? Arminian readers see God as the commander behind the disaster, calling the people to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s sovereignty over even destructive forces, which carry out his word. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing question as preparing for the call to repentance in 2:12.
